# Loops and conditionals

The human *BRCA1* transcript runs to 7,088 bases, and the protein it codes for
starts at base 114. Base 114 is an A, base 115 is a T, base 116 is a G. Read
through the rest of the transcript and the same three letters turn up 139 more
times. Nothing in the sequence marks which of the 140 the cell uses. So how
would you find all of them, and what would it take to pick the right one?

## Most ATGs are not start codons

Three letters is not much of a pattern. Four bases in the first position, four
in the second, four in the third: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 different three-letter words.
If bases turned up at random, about one position in 64 would spell ATG by
accident, and 7,088 ÷ 64 is about 111.

The real transcript has 140 of them, and real sequence isn't random, so the two
numbers were never going to agree. The estimate still does its job: a
three-letter pattern is short enough to turn up everywhere.

ATG codes for the amino acid methionine, and it does that wherever it appears.
Every methionine in the middle of a protein is an ATG in the sequence behind it.
A [start codon]{.term def="The ATG where translation begins. The same three
letters appear elsewhere in a gene and code methionine there instead."} isn't a
different word from those. It's the same word in a particular place.

The ribosome loads onto the front end of the messenger RNA, moves along, and
begins translating at the first ATG it meets. That's called the scanning model.
Position is what makes a start codon, and position is not a property of the
three letters.

ATG isn't formally the only one. NCBI's standard genetic code lists CTG and TTG
as start codons too, and Chapter 13 prints that table in full. This chapter
looks for ATG and nothing else, which is a decision I've made for you.

### One sequence, three ways to read it

Translation reads bases three at a time, with no gaps and no overlaps. Start at
base 114 and you get one set of codons. Start at 115 and every codon after it
is different, because each one has shifted by a base.

That choice is the [reading frame]{.term def="Which of the three ways of
chopping a sequence into triplets you are using. Shift by one base and every
codon changes."}. A DNA strand has three of them, and only one of them produces
the protein.

An ATG sitting 40 bases downstream of the real start never gets read as a word
at all. Divide 40 by 3 and you get 13 with 1 left over. That A is the second
base of a codon, the T closes that same codon, and the G opens the next one.
Three letters, two codons, no methionine.

::: {.why}
Annotating a new bacterial genome is this problem at scale: a few million bases
of continuous sequence, nothing labeled. The software that does it begins where
you're about to begin, by listing every start codon, and the rest of gene
finding is throwing most of that list away.
:::

## Doing the same thing to every position

Chapter 11 kept the first 200 bases in `brca1`, and this chapter needs all
7,088 of them. The cell below reads the file and puts the whole transcript into
that same variable.

```{python}
text = open("data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta").read()
lines = text.split(">")[1].splitlines()
brca1 = "".join(lines[1:])
print(lines[0])
print(len(brca1))
```

Two lines came back. The header names the record you got: this file holds five
species and the human transcript is only the first of them. Under the header is
7,088, the same number Chapter 5 read off the NCBI record, so the file is what
its name says.

Reading files properly is Chapter 15's job. The sequence stays in `brca1` for
the rest of the chapter, as long as the runtime doesn't disconnect.

A `for` loop runs the same lines of code once for each item you hand it. Here
the items come from `range(5)`, which hands out 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and then stops.

```{python}
for i in range(5):
    print(i, brca1[i])
```

`i` is an ordinary variable. The loop sets it to 0, runs the indented lines,
sets it to 1, and keeps going until `range` runs out. Indentation is the only
thing marking which lines belong to the loop, and Python has no closing bracket
to end one.

You asked for `range(5)` and got five numbers beginning at zero, so the last
one is four. That's the same off-by-one you met in Chapter 11.

Give `range` two numbers and it starts at the first and stops before the
second.

```{python}
for i in range(113, 116):
    print(i, brca1[i])
```

Those three bases are the start codon. Index 113 in Python is base 114 counting
from one, and converting between the two is the whole of Exercise 12.1.

::: {.check}
Run that loop. It prints `A`, then `T`, then `G`. If it prints `T`, `G`, `G`,
you fed the database's 114 straight into `range` as a Python index. Every
position you report for the rest of this chapter would then be one base to the
right of where it really is.
:::

A third number tells `range` how far to jump each time. Step by three and you
walk the sequence codon by codon, which is what the ribosome does.

```{python}
for i in range(113, 125, 3):
    print(i, brca1[i:i + 3])
```

Those are the first four codons of *BRCA1*, and you'll turn them into amino
acids in Chapter 13.

## Asking a question about each one

To find something, ask a question at each position and act only when the answer
is yes. The tool for that is `if`, and it runs its indented block only when the
test comes out true.

The test is usually a comparison. There are six of them.

| Operator | Asks |
|---|---|
| `==` | are these two equal |
| `!=` | are these two different |
| `<` | is the left one smaller |
| `>` | is the left one bigger |
| `<=` | smaller or equal |
| `>=` | bigger or equal |

Take a slice of three bases and compare it against the string `"ATG"`.

```{python}
i = 113
if brca1[i:i + 3] == "ATG":
    print("start codon at", i)
```

One equals sign assigns a value. Two equals signs ask a question.

`in` does two different jobs. Inside a `for` statement it means "take each item
from". On its own it asks whether one thing appears inside another.

```{python}
print("ATG" in brca1)
print("ATGATGATG" in brca1)
```

`True` and `False` are Python's two words for yes and no, and they're what a
comparison hands back when you print it instead of testing it. Both questions
are about the entire sequence. They won't tell you where or how many, which is
why you still need the loop.

The other comparison operators earn their keep when you want the biggest of
something. Walk 100 bases at a time, count the G and C in each window, and keep
two variables for the record holder. Overwrite both whenever the window in
front of you beats the record.

```{python}
best = 0
best_start = 0
for start in range(0, 500, 100):
    window = brca1[start:start + 100]
    gc = window.count("G") + window.count("C")
    print(start, gc)
    if gc > best:
        best = gc
        best_start = start
print(best_start, best)
```

The first five lines are the windows in the order they went past. The last line
is the record holder, and it stopped changing after the first pass: 59 at the
front, then nothing above 42. That stretch sits ahead of the start codon at
base 114 and repeats what Exercise 11.1 showed you on 40 bases.

Don't read it as a verdict on the whole transcript. You've looked at 500 bases
out of 7,088, and Exercise 12.2 slides this loop along all of them and turns up
a richer window a long way past the middle. Single letters can't overlap, so
`.count` is safe here.

## Walkthrough: every ATG in BRCA1

Now run the test at every position. The loop stops two bases early, because a
three-base slice taken from the last base has nothing to take.

```{python}
count = 0
for i in range(len(brca1) - 2):
    if brca1[i:i + 3] == "ATG":
        count = count + 1
print(count)
```

Your loop found 140 of them, in a transcript whose protein starts once.

Positions matter more than the total, so print them. This version stops at 500
to keep the output on the page.

```{python}
for i in range(500):
    if brca1[i:i + 3] == "ATG":
        print(i, i + 1)
```

The left column is Python's index and the right column is the base number a
database would give you. The top row is the real start codon. The nine rows
under it are ATGs that begin nothing.

The first ATG in the whole transcript is the one the cell uses, which is the
scanning model behaving as advertised. It isn't a rule you can lean on. Some
transcripts carry an ATG upstream of the real start.

Now cut the list down with the biology. Chapter 5 took the coding range off the
record as bases 114 to 5,705. Apply rule 2 from Chapter 11: the start moves to
113 and the stop stays at 5,705. Step through that range in threes and every
position you test begins a codon rather than sitting in the middle of one.

```{python}
count = 0
for i in range(113, 5705, 3):
    if brca1[i:i + 3] == "ATG":
        count = count + 1
print(count)
```

So 140 ATGs in the transcript, and 30 of them start a codon inside the coding
sequence. Those 30 are the ones the ribosome reads as a word, and each one puts
a methionine into the protein.

A second route to that 30 runs through Chapter 13. Translate the coding
sequence, count the letter M in the protein, and you get 30 again.

Picking the one of those 30 that starts the protein took something the sequence
doesn't contain. It took the coding range you read off the record in Chapter 5,
which NCBI built out of evidence somebody else collected. The loop finds the
pattern. What the pattern means is a separate job, and code won't settle it for
you.

### A shorter route that isn't the same route

A string method can count a pattern with no loop at all.

```{python}
count = 0
for i in range(len(brca1) - 1):
    if brca1[i:i + 2] == "AA":
        count = count + 1
print(brca1.count("ATG"), brca1.count("AA"), count)
```

`brca1.count("ATG")` agrees with your loop at 140. `brca1.count("AA")` says 634,
and the loop that tests every position says 883.

::: {.trap}
`.count` moves left to right, and after a match it carries on from the end of
that match rather than from the next base. So overlapping copies get skipped:
`"AAAA".count("AA")` returns 2 when three positions start an `AA`. ATG can't
overlap itself, which is the only reason `.count` agreed above. Neither answer
errors, and the wrong number looks exactly like the right one.
:::

Solutions are in the book's repository under `scripts/solutions/`. Work the
exercise first.

::: {.exercise num="12.1" time="25 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Find every ATG in the human *BRCA1* transcript and report where they are, in
both coordinate systems at once.
:::
::: {.given}
`brca1`, the 7,088-base string loaded at the top of this chapter. A match
counts wherever the three letters appear, including matches inside the
untranslated ends.
:::
::: {.produce}
One line per match, two numbers on it: the Python index, then the same position
counting from one. 140 lines, in ascending order.
:::
::: {.check}
Your first line reads `113 114`. The number 114 has to appear in the right-hand
column, because that's where the coding sequence starts. Chapter 5 took that
number off the database rather than out of your code, which is what makes it
worth checking against. If your right-hand column starts at 113 you printed the
index twice. If it starts at 115 you converted twice. Count your lines as well:
anything other than 140 means your `range` stopped in the wrong place.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="12.2" time="35 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Slide a window along the transcript, work out the GC content of each window,
and report the richest one. Do it for two window sizes.
:::
::: {.given}
`brca1` again. A window of 100 bases starting at every position in turn, then
the same thing with a window of 500. Several windows tie for the top score, so
keep the first one you meet and let a later window take the record only when it
scores strictly higher. Write your prediction down before you run anything.
When the window grows, what happens to the GC fraction you report? And what
happens to where in the transcript you find it?
:::
::: {.produce}
Two rows. Each row carries the window size, the 1-based start of the best
window, and its GC fraction rounded to two decimals. Plus the prediction you
made first.
:::
::: {.check}
The 100-base window starts at base 5,598 and scores 0.61. The 500-base window
starts at base 5,316 and scores 0.54. If your fractions match but your starts
sit further along, you kept the last tied window instead of the first, and
changing `>=` back to `>` moves them. One invariant catches the real bugs: a
500-base window is five 100-base windows averaged together, so its GC can never
beat the best 100-base window. If your longer window scores higher, the bug is
in your arithmetic and not in the biology.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="1.8in"}
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta'"}
Python is talking, and it's telling you where it looked. It searched the folder
the notebook is standing in and found nothing by that name. Either the data
folder isn't in this session yet or it sits somewhere other than the path says.
Nothing below this cell will run until it does, and Chapter 15 covers where a
notebook looks and how to point it somewhere else.
:::

::: {.errfix err="IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'for' statement on line 1"}
The line after your `for` isn't indented. Indentation is how Python knows which
lines belong to the loop, so a loop with nothing indented under it has no body.
Put four spaces at the front of every line the loop should repeat.
:::

::: {.errfix err="SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?"}
You wrote one equals sign inside an `if`. One assigns a value, two ask whether
two things match. Python guessed the fix and printed it inside the message.
Take the guess: change the `=` to `==` on the line the traceback names.
:::

::: {.errfix err="IndexError: string index out of range"}
You asked for a base past the end of the sequence. A loop that runs to
`len(brca1)` and then reads `brca1[i + 2]` runs off the end on its last two
passes. Stop the `range` early enough for the widest slice you take inside it.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Write a `for` loop over `range` and say what the loop variable holds on each
  pass
- Convert a list of Python indices into base numbers a database would
  recognize, and check one of them against a number you already have
- Explain why 140 ATGs in a transcript become 30 candidate codons and then one
  answer
- Say what `.count` does with overlapping matches, and name a pattern where
  that changes your answer
- Name the thing the annotation supplies that the sequence itself cannot
:::
